**Answer: Yes** (assuming $\dim M = \dim N$, which is necessary for "invertible" to even be meaningful). The differential $d_pF$ is invertible if and only if its coordinate matrix $D\hat F(\phi(p))$ is invertible, and this equivalence is independent of the choice of charts.

---

### Proof

Let $F:M\to N$ be a smooth map between smooth manifolds, $p\in M$, and let $(U,\phi)$, $(V,\psi)$ be charts with $p\in U$, $F(U)\subseteq V$. The **local representative** is
$$\hat F \;=\; \psi\circ F\circ \phi^{-1}:\phi(U)\longrightarrow\psi(V).$$
(We write the evaluation point as $\phi(p)$; the problem's notation $\psi(p)$ is the same object up to the naming of the source chart.)

**Coordinate bases.** The chart $\phi$ induces the basis $\bigl\{\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\big|_p\bigr\}_{i=1}^{m}$ of $T_pM$, and $\psi$ induces the basis $\bigl\{\tfrac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\big|_{F(p)}\bigr\}_{j=1}^{n}$ of $T_{F(p)}N$. By the chain rule,
$$d_pF\!\left(\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x^i}\bigg|_p\right) \;=\; \sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\partial \hat F^j}{\partial x^i}(\phi(p))\,\tfrac{\partial}{\partial y^j}\bigg|_{F(p)},$$
so the matrix of $d_pF$ in these coordinate bases is exactly the Jacobian $D\hat F(\phi(p))\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$.

---

**Step 1 — Equivalence for a fixed pair of charts.**

Assume $\dim M=\dim N=:d$. The map $d_pF:T_pM\to T_{F(p)}N$ is a linear map between $d$-dimensional real vector spaces. Choosing coordinate bases identifies $T_pM\cong\mathbb{R}^d$ and $T_{F(p)}N\cong\mathbb{R}^d$, and under these identifications $d_pF$ is represented by the matrix $D\hat F(\phi(p))$. A linear map between finite-dimensional spaces of equal dimension is an isomorphism **iff** its matrix (in any fixed pair of bases) is invertible. Hence
$$d_pF \text{ is invertible} \;\iff\; D\hat F(\phi(p)) \text{ is invertible}.$$

---

**Step 2 — Chart independence.**

Let $(\tilde U,\tilde\phi)$, $(\tilde V,\tilde\psi)$ be another pair of charts around $p$ and $F(p)$. The new local representative is
$$\widetilde{\hat F} \;=\; \tilde\psi\circ F\circ\tilde\phi^{-1} \;=\; \underbrace{(\tilde\psi\circ\psi^{-1})}_{\text{transition on }N}\circ\;\hat F\;\circ\underbrace{(\phi\circ\tilde\phi^{-1})}_{\text{transition on }M}.$$
Applying the chain rule at $\tilde\phi(p)$:
$$D\widetilde{\hat F}(\tilde\phi(p)) \;=\; \underbrace{D(\tilde\psi\circ\psi^{-1})\bigl(\psi(F(p))\bigr)}_{=:\,A}\;\cdot\; D\hat F(\phi(p))\;\cdot\;\underbrace{D(\phi\circ\tilde\phi^{-1})(\tilde\phi(p))}_{=:\,B}.$$
The transition maps $\tilde\psi\circ\psi^{-1}$ and $\phi\circ\tilde\phi^{-1}$ are diffeomorphisms between open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^d$, so their derivatives $A$ and $B$ are **invertible** $d\times d$ matrices. Therefore
$$\det D\widetilde{\hat F}(\tilde\phi(p)) \;=\; \det(A)\,\det\!\bigl(D\hat F(\phi(p))\bigr)\,\det(B),$$
with $\det A\neq 0$ and $\det B\neq 0$. Consequently
$$\det D\widetilde{\hat F}(\tilde\phi(p))\neq 0 \;\iff\; \det D\hat F(\phi(p))\neq 0.$$
So invertibility of the coordinate matrix is **preserved under any change of charts**.

---

**Step 3 — Combining the two steps.**

For any choice of charts, by Step 1,
$$d_pF \text{ invertible} \;\iff\; D\hat F(\phi(p)) \text{ invertible},$$
and by Step 2 the right-hand side is independent of which charts are used. Therefore the equivalence
$$\boxed{\,d_pF \text{ is invertible} \;\iff\; D\hat F(\phi(p)) \text{ is invertible}\,}$$
holds **regardless of the choice of charts**, provided $\dim M=\dim N$.

---

**Remark on the equal-dimension hypothesis.** If $\dim M\neq\dim N$, then $d_pF$ maps between spaces of different dimensions and cannot be a (two-sided) isomorphism; likewise the Jacobian is a non-square matrix and cannot be invertible. Both sides are then simply false, so the equivalence is vacuous. The meaningful statement requires $\dim M=\dim N$, under which the proof above gives the result. $\blacksquare$
